caseno:
Appeal from Original Decree No. 47 of 1990
with
Appeal from Original Order No. 124 of 1990
lawyer:
Habibul Islam Bhuiyan with A Khaleque, Advocates ----- For the Appellant. 
Farid Ahmed, Assistant Attorney-General ----- For the Respondent
parties:
Titas Prokaushali Limited ----- Appellant
Vs.
Roads and Highways Department, Government of Bangladesh ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
Md. Mozammel Haque J: Since two appeals, namely, FA No. 47 of 1990 and FMA No. 124 of 1990 have arisen out of one judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 8 of 1985 and Miscellaneous Case No. 981 of 1984 by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka, they are heard together and disposed of by the one judgment. 

 2. The facts relevant for the purpose of this case are, that for conduction of bridges and culverts in Comilla-Chandina by-pass project, Government received funds from the International Development Association (IDA), and the Roads and Highways Department of the Government invited tenders on 16.4.80. Titas Prokaushali Limited (TPL), namely, the present appellant submitted tenders along with others for the aforesaid works and being lowest, the appellant got the said works under two contracts known as BC-1(for construction of bridges) and BC-2 (for construction of culverts.) During the construction works on the aforesaid two contracts, several disputes were raised and TPL, namely, the appellant, suffered losses and for that reason they lodged claims during the execution of the works. As par terms of the contracts the disputes, which are 20 in number, were referred by the appellant to the Engineer, a Foreign Consultant, engaged by the Government for supervision of the works, as per conditions of the contract, for decision of the engineer under relevant heads. The Consultant Engineer gave his decisions on the 20 claims lodged by the appellant and being dissatisfied with the decisions of the Consultant Engineer, the appellant wanted to refer the matter for arbitration as per terms of the contract. Ultimately, both the parties agreed to refer the disputes to arbitration and as a result the arbitration entered into a reference on 2.8.84. 

 3. On 25.8.84 the appellant filed the aforesaid 20 disputes before the Arbitrators with amendment of the claimed-amount in claim No. 1 only of Be-1, and BC-2, Before the Arbitrators the Government filed the written statement on 4.9.84. On 5.9.84 the Arbitrators framed the issues. Thereafter the Arbitrators took evidence of both the parties, heard the arguments and on perusal of the papers and documents on records unanimously gave an award on 10.11.84. It appears that in total the appellant submitted a claim to the Arbitrators for a sum of Taka 1,62,56,189.00. Ultimately, after hearing the parties and perusing the materials on record the Arbitrators gave an award for a sum of Taka 90,52,986.00 in addition to Taka 1,58,097.00 as given by the Consultant Engineer. After passing the aforesaid award the appellant submitted the award before the learned Subordinate Judge for making it a Rule of Court as required under section 14 of the Arbitration Act. As against the award the Roads and Highways Department, the respondent, also filed a case, namely, Miscellaneous Case No. 981 of 1984 in the 3rd Court of the learned Subordinate Judge Dhaka, dated 29.11.80 under section 38 of the Arbitration Act. The presentation of the award before the learned Subordinate Judge was registered as Title Suit No. 8 of 1985. Since this Title Suit No. 8 of 1985 and the Miscellaneous Case No. 981 of 1984 had arisen out of the same award, the learned Subordinate Judge heard both the-cases together and disposed of them by giving one judgment which is before us under challenge. The learned Subordinate Judge, after hearing the parties and considering the materials on record, passed his judgment on 29.11.89 by which the Title Suit No. 8 of 1985 was dismissed and Miscellaneous Case No. 981 of 1984 was allowed and as a result the award of the Arbitrators dated 18.11.84 was set aside. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge in the aforesaid two cases the above appeals have been preferred, one with regard to Title Suit No. 8 of 1985 and the other with regard to Miscellaneous Case No. 981 of 1984. 

 4. From the judgment it appears that the award was set aside by the learned Subordinate Judge on two counts. Firstly, the claims within the contracts must have to be lodged within 30 days from the date of cause of action before the Consultant Engineer as per terms 67(1) of the Contract Since the claims lodged to the Consultant Engineer were beyond the period of 30 days, the terms of the contract have been violated and, as such, the learned Subordinate Judge held that the Arbitrators misconducted themselves in giving the award. Secondly, the amounts claimed in 20 disputes before the Consultant Engineer were raised before the Arbitrators. Since the claims made before the Arbitrators were higher than the claims made before the Consultant Engineer, the award has been vitiated and, as such, the learned Subordinate Judge set aside the award. The respondent-Government raised some other points before the learned Subordinate Judge, but the same were not accepted. Mainly on two counts as stated above the award was set aside by the learned Subordinate Judge. From the judgment it appears that learned Subordinate Judge held that the Arbitrators have misconducted themselves in passing the award and this misconduct was a legal misconduct. There was no finding as to the personal misconduct of the Arbitrators. 

 5. Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, submits that the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of law in his judgment inasmuch as though the Arbitrators had acted within the bounds of the two contracts and not outside the contracts, the learned Judge illegally set aside the award by the impugned judgment and, as such, the impugned judgment is liable to be set aside. He further submits that all the disputes arose within the limit of the two contracts. Since the Arbitrators had not crossed the limit of the bounds of the contracts and since the Arbitrators had not done or decided or held anything in the award which is totally contrary to any existing provisions of law, the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge cannot be sustained in law. Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that the Court has no authority to set aside the award of the Arbitrators on merit however erroneous or irregular it may be. Only the Court is entitled to set aside an award on the ground of legal misconduct or personal misconduct of the Arbitrators. The provisions for setting aside an award have been incorporated in section 30 of the Arbitration Act which runs as follows: 

 (a) that an arbitrator or umpire has misconducted himself or the proceedings; 

 In interpreting the section it comes to us that an award can be set aside by a court of law only on the ground of legal misconduct or personal misconduct of the Arbitrators or the umpire as the case may be. 

 6. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that it is alleged in the impugned Judgment that the terms as contained in condition No. 67(1) of the contract had been violated allegedly on the ground that within 30 days from the date of cause of action the disputes were not lodged to the Consultant Engineer. Since terms of contract were violated, the award was set aside. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that this is absolutely a misconception of law, in view of the fact that the Arbitrators had not gone beyond the limit of the contract. During the contract works several exigencies took place as a result of which the appellant lodged claims to the Consultant Engineer. In total 20 claims were lodged to the consultant, but the same were not rejected on the ground that those were not placed before him beyond time; rather some of them were accepted in part and some others were rejected on their own merit, according to the Consultant Engineer. But no ground has been shown that those were placed before him after due time. There might be some irregularities or laches or lapses in performance of the terms and conditions of the contract in between the parties during the contract works, but that is within the periphery and ambit of the contract. Since those disputes had been raised within the bounds of the contract and not beyond the contract, we are of the view that on such ground a Court cannot set aside an award inasmuch as in order to resolve such disputes the parties jointly-referred the matters to arbitration. If such ground is allowed, it will amount to interference into the merit of the award which the Court is not competent to do. It appears from the judgment as well as from the award submitted before us that the 20 disputes arose within the periphery of the two contracts and in order to resolve above claims and disputes both the parties jointly referred those disputes to the Arbitrators. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Additional Attorney-General, was the Arbitrator for the Government and Md. Jamiruddin Sirkar, Bar-at-Law, an Advocate of the Supreme Court, was the Arbitrator for the appellant. 

 10. As regards the sanctity and propriety of an award passed under the Arbitration Act, particularly with regard to an "unanimous award", Mr. Habibul Islam Bhuiyan has referred to several decisions of the Higher Courts of this Sub-Continent. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that section 30 of the Arbitration Act starts with a negative compulsion clause, namely, "an award shall not be set aside excepting on one or more of the following grounds," that means a compulsion in negative terms has been added which means that beside in exceptional cases an award of the Arbitrators should not be touched. He has referred to the case of Smt. Santa Shaila Devi. Vs. Dhirendra Nath Sen, AIR 1963 (SC), 1677. In the aforesaid judgment it was described as to what would be the attitude of the Court towards an award. It was held there that the Court attitude must always be to support it and not to destroy it. Two other decisions reported in AIR 1924 (All.) 800 and AIR (Bom) 296 show that court of law should not touch the award on merit. The Court can only touch the award if it can be shown that there was legal or personal misconduct of the Arbitrators, because in an arbitration the parties must choose their own judges at their own choice and they must be bound by the decision of their own judges. It means, neither of the parties can retract from its own judgment. Court cannot substitute the reasonings of the Arbitrators. Nowhere in the whole judgment the learned. Subordinate Judge has found anything to the effect that the Arbitrators went beyond the reference or contract or the issues which relate to the two contracts made between the parties. Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that mere criticism of the award, however strong it may be, will not vitiate the award and in support of this contention be has referred to the case of Kripa Sindhu Biswas Vs. Sudha Biswas, AIR 1973 (Cal) 496. In the judgment of the case of Fazal and others Vs. State 43 DLR 41, a single Bench of this Court held that the Court which is required to make the award a Rule of the Court and before whom the application under section 30 of the Arbitration Act is filed is not a Court of appeal. Having participated in the arbitration of their own accord the parties cannot raise any dispute as to the issues before the Arbitrators which are decided unanimously. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that the main two objections as were not in fact raised and agitated before the Arbitrators and for the first time they were agitated before the learned Subordinate Judge and, as such, no issue was framed by the Arbitrators on such points. Mr. Bhuiyan has referred to the case of Ghulam Abbas Vs. Trustees of the Port of Karachi PLD 1987 (SC) 393 wherein it was held by their Lordships that even if the award is wrong, even then it cannot be the subject of review by the Court. Arbitrators are the judges in all questions of facts as well as law and, as such, the decision of the Arbitrators should not be interfered with by the Court. In the decision reported in AIR 1963 (SC) it is held by their Lordships that in a proceeding of setting aside an award it is not open to the Court to reappreciate the evidence and to sit in appeal over the conclusion the Arbitrators arrived at. In the case of the President of Union of India Vs. Kalinga Construction Ltd, AIR 1971 (SC) 1946, it is held that objection against an award is not to be heard as if it were an appeal against the decision of the Arbitrators. 

 11. Upshot of all the above decisions appears to us that when an award is unanimously passed by the Arbitrators the court of law shall not interfere in it except in a very rare case where the Arbitrators have misconducted themselves on any legal point or in the personal dealings. As regards legal misconduct we are of the view that if the Arbitrators have done anything in deciding the matter or in passing the award contrary to any specific provision of law, that can be treated as legal misconduct. Further, this legal misconduct can be extended to the extent that if the Arbitrators have done anything beyond the contract or beyond the reference or beyond the issues, in that case also it can be termed as legal misconduct. As to personal misconduct we are of the view that it relates to the personal dealings of the Arbitrators in conducting the proceeding of an award in a case. In the present case there is no finding as to personal misconduct; rather there is finding of legal misconduct. So, considering the materials on record and the judicial pronouncements on arbitration award as referred to above, we hold that there having been no legal misconduct of the arbitrators the learned Subordinate Judge illegally set aside the award in question and, as such, his judgment cannot be sustained. 

 12. Mr. Bhuiyan further submits that at the time of filing objection against the award under section 30 of the Arbitration Act the aggrieved party must file an application with security of at least 50% of the awarded amount, but in the present case when the application under section 30 of the Arbitration Act was filed before the learned Subordinate Judge no such security was given rather, the Superintending Engineer on behalf of the Government had given an undertaking with the application. Subsequently, the Government ratified the undertaking of the Superintending Engineer beyond the period of 30 days. He submits that such undertaking docs not fulfil the requirements of the provisions of section 30 as amended. It appears that on 9.2.84 the Superintending Engineer had submitted an undertaking on behalf of the present respondent which was subsequently ratified by the Ministry of Communication, Government of Bangladesh on 24.11.88 by a Memorandum. Mr. Bhuiyan submits that such an undertaking is not a legal security as contemplated under the law. So-called ratification by the Government came long after the period of limitation and, as such, this undertaking cannot be accepted. A similar argument was advanced before the learned Subordinate Judge. It is true that the Superintending Engineer had given an undertaking at the time of filing of the application under section 30 of the Arbitration Act. Security means that it must be something positive to be placed before the Court on which the party can easily realise the amount through Court if it is decided in its favour. In the present case the undertaking was given by the Superintending Engineer on behalf of the Government which was subsequently ratified by the Ministry. Since Government is that party here which filed the application under section 30 of the Arbitration Act and since such a responsible officer of the Government had given an undertaking on behalf of the Government which was subsequently ratified by the Ministry of the Government, in the peculiar circumstances of this particular case, we hold, it can be treated as a sufficient security and compliance of the provisions of law. In that regard the findings of the learned Subordinate Judge do not require any interference by us; rather we find that the findings are very much cogent, reasonable and legal. So this objection of Mr. Bhuiyan has no substance. 

 14. Arbitrator is not a court and arbitration proceeding is not a court proceeding. Bangali meaning of the word arbitration is “সালিশ”. In our view, such Salish is some sort of endeavour for amicable settlement of the disputes in between the parties through the arbitrators (Salishdars) without going to' the Court. It is not required to follow all the procedures of a legal proceeding like a Court of law. It is same thing like voluntary give and take in between the parties without entering into legal proceeding in a Court of law for speedy benefit or relief to the parties who mutually agree upon to do it. So, the Court must not touch the award except on the ground of misconduct of the Arbitrators or umpire. 

 15. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the materials on record, we are of the view that the learned Subordinate Judge has committed an error of law in setting aside the unanimous award in question in view of the fact that he failed to show any legal misconduct on the part of the Arbitrators. If on such flimsy grounds, which were not even agitated before the Arbitrators, an award is allowed to be set aside, then we are afraid, the sanctity of the award given under law cannot be safeguarded. We disapprove of such attitude of the Court in view of the fact that the Court does not sit as a Court of appeal over the award and it cannot touch the award on merit. But in the present case we find the learned Subordinate Judge has touched the award on merit by usurping the functions of the arbitrators. Such an action without jurisdiction is totally disapproved by us. 

 In the result, both the appeals are allowed and the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 8 of 1985 along with Miscellaneous Case No. 981 of 1984 are hereby set aside. In respect of Title Suit No. 8 of 1985, left the award be made Rule of the Court and Miscellaneous Case No. 981 of 1984 is dismissed. The trial Court is directed to draw up the decree in accordance with law.
